title: Finding duplicate files without changing them

parts.text: A duplicate reporter answers a narrow question: which regular files yielded the same byte content during a scan? It does not decide which copy you should keep. A matching name is not evidence of matching content. Different names can contain identical bytes.

Use two filters: first group by byte size, then hash only groups with more than one member. A hash maps an arbitrary byte sequence to a fixed-size digest. Equal bytes produce equal SHA-256 digests; equal digests are extremely strong evidence, but are not a mathematical proof of equal bytes. A byte-for-byte comparison is the stricter next step when the distinction matters.

Observation	What it supports	What it does not establish
Same filename	Similar naming	Same content
Same size	Possible duplicate	Same content
Same SHA-256	Strong content-match evidence	Independent physical copies

Hard links can name the same underlying file. Symbolic links point elsewhere and this project skips them. A file can also change between the size check and reading. This first version assumes you scan a quiet folder you control; it is not designed for hostile filesystem races.

Reading in chunks bounds the byte buffer, although the program still stores file paths and grouping metadata. The digest state is updated in order with every chunk. Do not hash just the first chunk and call it a whole-file fingerprint.
References: pathlib, hashlib. Continue with the implementation or the learning Journey.

learningShape.subject: Finding duplicate files without changing them

parts.text: Save this as duplicates.py and run it with Python 3.10 or later. It prints JSON arrays of paths that have equal observed sizes and SHA-256 digests. It scans regular files below the chosen root, skips symlinks, and reports readable filesystem errors on stderr. It never edits scanned files.

Invoke it as python duplicates.py /path/to/a/quiet/folder. Empty files form a valid duplicate group. Errors produce incomplete results, not a claim that skipped files are unique. A path containing a symlink in a parent component is not excluded by the root check; choose the root yourself and do not treat these checks as a security boundary.
This code is a learning baseline. It does not detect mutation during reads or deduplicate hard links by inode. Those limitations are part of the content model.

title: Build and inspect a duplicate report

parts.text: Read the model. Write down why two equal-size files might still differ. Predict how empty files will behave.
Save the program as duplicates.py. In the same directory, save this as try_duplicates.py. It creates and removes only its own temporary fixture directory; the reporter remains read-only.

from pathlib import Path
import subprocess
import sys
import tempfile

with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory(prefix="duplicate-demo-") as folder:
    root = Path(folder)
    (root / "one.txt").write_bytes(b"same\n")
    (root / "two.txt").write_bytes(b"same\n")
    (root / "other.txt").write_bytes(b"else\n")
    (root / "empty-a").write_bytes(b"")
    (root / "empty-b").write_bytes(b"")
    subprocess.run([sys.executable, "duplicates.py", str(root)], check=True)

Run python try_duplicates.py from the directory containing both scripts. The expected group memberships are one.txt with two.txt, and empty-a with empty-b. other.txt has the same size as the two text duplicates but different bytes. Temporary path prefixes vary. This expected result is a prediction, not a record of execution.
• Identify the line that skips hashing singleton size groups.

• Edit the fixture source line for two.txt: replace b"same\n" with b"sane\n", preserving its byte length. Then rerun try_duplicates.py; each run creates a new temporary directory, and the previous directory is already gone.
• Explain why a missing group after a permission error cannot establish uniqueness.

To reproduce a read failure without depending on operating-system permissions, save this as try_failure.py beside duplicates.py and run it. It injects PermissionError only when the reporter fingerprints two.txt; it does not change real permissions. Predict which duplicate group becomes incomplete and inspect stderr for the reported error.

from pathlib import Path
import tempfile
from unittest.mock import patch
import duplicates

with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory(prefix="failure-demo-") as folder:
    root = Path(folder)
    for name in ("one.txt", "two.txt"):
        (root / name).write_bytes(b"same")
    original = duplicates.fingerprint
    def injected(path):
        if path.name == "two.txt":
            raise PermissionError("synthetic read failure")
        return original(path)
    with patch.object(duplicates, "fingerprint", side_effect=injected):
        print(duplicates.duplicates(root))
The missing complete group cannot establish that these files differ. The failure was injected before reading one candidate, so that candidate has no digest evidence.
Checkpoint: Describe one input assumption and one output limitation before adapting this tool to your own folder.
Add a final byte comparison, or record file metadata before and after hashing and flag changes. Neither extension makes a live filesystem into a snapshot. Keep deletion outside this project.

parts.text: A cache stores an answer so that later requests can avoid repeating work. The authoritative source determines the current price; the cache holds a previously computed price. A dictionary can implement either role. Its role depends on the system’s contract, not its data structure.
A cache hit means a usable entry exists for a key. It does not mean the answer matches the source right now. On a miss, a cache-aside reader loads the source and stores the answer.

rows: Limits how long an entry is eligible for reuse
Notifications may be delayed or lost
Caller must obtain the right version

parts.text:
Mechanism	Benefit	Limit
Time-to-live (TTL)	Limits how long an entry is eligible for reuse	Source may change before expiry
Explicit invalidation	Removes a known stale entry	Notifications may be delayed or lost
Versioned key	Separates versions of an answer	Caller must obtain the right version

For a cache loaded at time 0 with TTL 10, a source change at time 2 can leave the old value served until time 10. TTL alone does not provide freshness at every read. A monotonic clock is appropriate for elapsed durations because wall-clock corrections should not extend or shorten a local deadline unexpectedly.

A key must include every input that can change the answer under the cache’s contract. For a shop price, this may include product, currency, customer segment, and region. Omitting currency can return a syntactically valid number with the wrong meaning. Storing a missing-item result is negative caching; it needs its own freshness policy too.

A cache is useful only when its cost and freshness tradeoffs fit the task. Independent processes also need a policy for concurrent misses and invalidation; a local dictionary does not coordinate them.
Reference: time.monotonic. Explore the deterministic demonstration and reasoning Journey.

title: Observe expiry with a fake clock

parts.text: This standard-library Python example models one process and one price key. Fake time makes the expiry boundary visible without sleeping. Amounts use integer cents to avoid introducing floating-point money arithmetic.

class PriceCache:
    def __init__(self, load, now, ttl):
        if ttl < 0:
            raise ValueError("ttl must be non-negative")
        self.load = load
        self.now = now
        self.ttl = ttl
        self.entries = {}

    def get(self, key):
        entry = self.entries.get(key)
        if entry is not None:
            expires_at, value = entry
            if self.now() < expires_at:
                return value
        value = self.load(key)
        self.entries[key] = (self.now() + self.ttl, value)
        return value

    def invalidate(self, key):
        self.entries.pop(key, None)

clock = [0]
key = ("mug", "USD", "retail")
source = {key: 1200}
cache = PriceCache(source.__getitem__, lambda: clock[0], ttl=10)
print(cache.get(key))
source[key] = 1500
clock[0] = 9
print(cache.get(key))
clock[0] = 10
print(cache.get(key))
source[key] = 1700
cache.invalidate(key)
print(cache.get(key))

The predicted output is 1200, 1200, 1500, then 1700, each on its own line. The comparison uses <, so an entry expires exactly at its deadline. This text records an expected result, not an executed run. TTL begins after loading completes. In a real local implementation, inject time.monotonic for elapsed-time deadlines.

The implementation has no capacity limit, thread coordination, negative caching, or persistence. A failed load raises and does not install a new entry; after expiry, an old entry remains stored but is ineligible for reuse. For the policy behind those choices, see the cache model.

parts.text: Read the cache model. Draw a two-column notebook trace: authoritative price and cached price. At time 0, load 1200 cents. Change the source to 1500 at time 2. Predict the value at times 9 and 10 under a TTL of 10. Explain why the entry’s age and the source’s age are different concepts.

Run the fake-clock example locally. Compare its output to your trace. Change the TTL to zero and explain why every call loads the source, even though entries are still stored. No real delay or network request is needed.

Your shop introduces member discounts and prices in EUR. List the dimensions of the answer before choosing a tuple key. Give an example of two requests that would collide under a product-only key but should produce different prices.
Checkpoint: State the freshness promise you would make to a shopper. “Fast” is a performance goal; it is not a freshness promise.

Two workers miss the same key at once. Describe the redundant work they might do. Then consider a source update arriving while an old load is still running. What evidence would you need before claiming invalidation prevents all stale writes? Keep that as a design question; this single-process demonstration does not answer it.

title: What a composite index might change

parts.text: Consider events with an integer identifier, a device identifier, an integer timestamp, and a payload. The query filters on one device and asks for the newest rows with an explicit tie-breaker:

SELECT id, recorded_at, payload
FROM events
WHERE device_id = ?
ORDER BY recorded_at DESC, id DESC
LIMIT 20;

An index on (device_id, recorded_at DESC, id DESC) may let SQLite seek to the relevant device and read rows in the requested order. Without a suitable index, SQLite may scan more rows and use a temporary structure for ordering. The actual choice depends on available indexes, statistics, data, and SQLite version.

An index stores additional data and must be maintained on writes. The proposed index does not contain payload, so it is not a covering index for this query: fetching a result’s payload can require looking up the table row. “Uses an index” and “is faster for this workload” are different observations.

The id tie-breaker makes the ordering deterministic when timestamps match. Parameter binding separates SQL structure from parameter values. The in-memory experiment does not model durable disk writes, production cache conditions, or every device distribution.
References: SQLite query planning, EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN, Python sqlite3. See the experiment Journey and open Investigation.

learningShape.subject: What a composite index might change

title: Compare a query before and after indexing

parts.text: Read the index model. Predict whether an index that starts with device_id can reduce work for the filtered, ordered query. Write a competing explanation: a small table might already be fast enough that index maintenance is not worthwhile.

This script uses only Python’s standard library and creates an in-memory database. Save it as index_probe.py and run python index_probe.py. It prints the local SQLite version, plans, median warm-query time, and number of returned rows. No execution results are supplied here. The timestamp i // 1000 deliberately gives multiple rows of the same device the same timestamp. The assertions check equal results before/after, descending (recorded_at, id) order, and the presence of a timestamp tie in the returned rows.

import sqlite3
import statistics
import time

query = """SELECT id, recorded_at, payload FROM events
WHERE device_id = ?
ORDER BY recorded_at DESC, id DESC LIMIT 20"""

def measure(connection, label):
    plan = connection.execute(
        "EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN " + query, (7,)
    ).fetchall()
    connection.execute(query, (7,)).fetchall()
    samples = []
    rows = []
    for _ in range(30):
        started = time.perf_counter()
        rows = connection.execute(query, (7,)).fetchall()
        samples.append(time.perf_counter() - started)
    print(label, plan)
    print("median seconds:", statistics.median(samples))
    print("rows:", len(rows))
    return rows

with sqlite3.connect(":memory:") as connection:
    print("SQLite", sqlite3.sqlite_version)
    connection.execute("""CREATE TABLE events (
        id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, device_id INTEGER NOT NULL,
        recorded_at INTEGER NOT NULL, payload TEXT NOT NULL)""")
    connection.executemany(
        "INSERT INTO events VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?)",
        ((i, i % 100, i // 1000, "sample") for i in range(1, 50001)),
    )
    connection.commit()
    before = measure(connection, "before")
    connection.execute("""CREATE INDEX event_device_time
        ON events(device_id, recorded_at DESC, id DESC)""")
    connection.commit()
    after = measure(connection, "after")
    if before != after:
        raise RuntimeError("result mismatch")
    if after != sorted(after, key=lambda row: (row[1], row[0]), reverse=True):
        raise RuntimeError("ordering mismatch")
    if not any(left[1] == right[1] for left, right in zip(after, after[1:])):
        raise RuntimeError("fixture did not exercise timestamp ties")

Keep the version, both plans, timings, input size, and whether the row comparison passed. A plan describes the selected access strategy; it does not count rows actually examined. This script does not measure rows examined, and a changed plan alone cannot establish that fewer rows were visited. Plan descriptions are diagnostic output whose text can change between SQLite versions; do not parse them as a stable API. Repeated queries mostly measure warm conditions, and running the indexed case second introduces an order effect.

Repeat at smaller and larger row counts, and with a skewed device distribution. For a concrete order check, refactor database creation and population into a function that returns a fresh connection with identical generated rows, and make the measurement function return all 30 samples as well as rows. In round 1 create two separate databases: measure an unindexed database first, then create the index on the second database and measure it. Close both. In round 2 recreate both from scratch, measure the indexed database first, then the unindexed database. Repeat paired rounds, alternating order, with the same query parameters and one warm-up query per measured case. Keep every per-query sample with its round, case, row count, and case order; compare medians, tails, and within-case spread rather than retaining only a single aggregate. Do not include population or index-creation time in query samples; measure those costs separately if relevant. This controls the obvious shared-database order effect but still measures warm in-memory queries and cannot remove every host-load effect. To study write cost or file size, design a separate disposable file-backed experiment; the script above does not measure them. Add observations to the open Investigation, preserving uncertainty.

title: Open Investigation: should the event log gain an index?

parts.text: Would a composite device/time index improve the intended event-log workload enough to justify extra storage and write maintenance? Unanswered. No local or production experiment has been executed for this record. No timing, plan, or storage result is claimed.

1. The proposed index enables a more selective access path and avoids a separate sort for the target query, making representative reads faster. Plans can support the access-path claim; proving fewer rows were actually examined requires separate execution instrumentation, which this experiment does not provide.
2. The table is small or the query infrequent enough that the practical benefit is negligible.
3. Read gains exist, but write maintenance or storage cost makes the overall tradeoff unattractive.

rows: Establishes what access paths were selected
Tests costs omitted by the memory demo
Realistic device skew and payload sizes

parts.text:
Evidence	Status	Why it matters
Version and plans before/after	Not collected	Establishes what access paths were selected
Representative read latency distribution	Not collected	Measures the user-facing query cost
Read and write frequency	Unknown	Weighs benefit against maintenance
File-backed write and size measurements	Not collected	Tests costs omitted by the memory demo
Realistic device skew and payload sizes	Unknown	Checks whether synthetic data transfers

Before running experiments, choose a read-latency target and acceptable write/storage budget appropriate to the application. A changed plan is supporting evidence; meeting those workload goals is the decision criterion. If the baseline already meets the target with margin, that weakens the urgency to add an index. If results vary widely, investigate the variance before choosing a winner.

Run the disposable experiment, attach the actual observations, and revise these hypotheses. Keep the reusable index explanation separate from measured claims. Do not convert a prediction into a conclusion merely because the proposed index sounds plausible.
